## Rating

::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple" title="Met"}
Code, and where feasible data, is kept in a version-controlled repository (e.g. Git on GitHub/GitLab) with its history accessible, and the exact version used for the paper is identified (a tagged release, commit hash, or archived snapshot with a DOI, e.g. via Zenodo).
:::
::: {.callout-warning appearance="simple" title="Partially met"}
The code is under version control, but the version used for the paper is not identified (only the current state of a branch), or only a snapshot without its history is shared.
:::
::: {.callout-important appearance="simple" title="Not met"}
No version control is used; files are shared only as static copies without history or version identifier.
:::

[Based on: [#3](../../sources.qmd#p3 "Reproducing statistical results") access to future updates, [#4](../../sources.qmd#p4 "Storing reproducible results from computational experiments using scientific python packages") git revision captured as metadata, [#54](../../sources.qmd#p54 "WORCS: a workflow for open reproducible code in science")/[#63](../../sources.qmd#p63 "Toward practical transparent verifiable and long-term reproducible research using guix")/[#108](../../sources.qmd#p108 "Checklists for computational reproducibility in social sciences: insights from literature and survey evaluation")/[#131](../../sources.qmd#p131 "Guide for Accelerating Computational Reproducibility in the Social Sciences") Git, [#69](../../sources.qmd#p69 "The interdependence of data producers and data users: how researchers’ behaviors can support or hinder each other") versioning and tracking of data and code, [#38](../../sources.qmd#p38 "Ten simple rules for writing dockerfiles for reproducible data science") Dockerfile under version control.]{.source-note}

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple" title="Not applicable"}
Never.
:::
